questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) What are hot spots?

(2 marks)

(ii) Subduction zones are areas of recycling where all the processes of the rock cycle can be realised. Assess the validity of this statement.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Hot spots.** A hot spot is a **fixed, long-lived area of unusually high heat flow and volcanic activity at the Earth's surface**, which lies **above a mantle plume**, a narrow column of **hot rock rising from deep in the mantle**. It is **independent of the plate boundaries** (most are within plates, a few on a ridge, e.g. Iceland). As the **plate moves over the stationary plume, a chain of volcanoes** is formed, which is **older with distance from the active hot spot** (the Hawaiian-Emperor chain; Yellowstone).

**(ii) Assessment of the statement.** The statement is **largely valid**, because a subduction zone (the trench, the subducting slab, the mantle wedge and the volcanic arc or mountain belt above it) is the one tectonic setting where **igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary processes are all concentrated and linked together**:

1. **Sedimentary processes (weathering, erosion, transport, deposition, lithification).** The volcanic arc and the uplifted mountain chain are **weathered and eroded**, and the rivers carry the sediment to the **trench, fore-arc and back-arc basins**, where thick sequences (greywackes, turbidites) are **deposited and lithified** by burial; the **sediments of the ocean floor are scraped off to form an accretionary wedge**.
2. **Metamorphism.** The subducting oceanic crust and sediments are carried down to **increasing pressure with relatively low temperature**, so that they are **metamorphosed** to **blueschist and then eclogite** (high-pressure metamorphism), while **contact and regional metamorphism** takes place round the rising magma and in the thickened crust of the arc.
3. **Melting and igneous activity.** The water that is **released from the slab** (dehydration of the metamorphic minerals) lowers the melting point of the **mantle wedge**, causing **partial melting** which produces magma. This **rises to form andesitic volcanoes (extrusive rocks) and granitic and dioritic plutons (intrusive rocks)** in the arc.
4. **Recycling.** The rock of the surface (oceanic crust, sediments, water, carbon) is **taken down and partly melted, and returned to the surface as new igneous rock**, so **old crust is destroyed and new continental crust is made**: material is truly recycled, completing the loop sediment, metamorphic rock, magma, igneous rock, sediment.

**Limits to the statement (why it is not wholly valid).**

- The word "**all**" is too strong if "subduction zone" means only the **trench and the slab**: **weathering, erosion and deposition happen at the surface of the arc and basins**, not in the subduction zone itself, and not all of the material is returned, since part of the **slab sinks deep into the mantle** for a long time.
- The rock cycle is **not confined to subduction zones**: it also operates, **wholly or in part, at other settings**, such as divergent boundaries and hot spots (igneous), continental collision zones, passive margins and cratons (sedimentary) and around any intrusion (contact metamorphism). It is **not a single circular path**: rocks can take **short cuts** (igneous rock straight to metamorphic rock, or to a new sedimentary rock).

**Conclusion.** Subduction zones are among the **most complete and important areas of rock recycling**, since every process of the cycle occurs in the whole subduction system (trench, slab, wedge and arc), but they are **not the only places** and the statement is valid **only if the subduction zone is taken as the whole convergent-margin system**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Differentiate between a joint and a fault.

(3 marks)

(ii) Name and describe TWO Features found in fault zones.

(6 marks)

(iii) How can faults be dated?

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Joint and fault.**

| | **Joint** | **Fault** |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | a **fracture in a rock along which there has been no displacement (or negligible movement) of the two sides parallel to the fracture**; the walls have only moved apart, if at all | a **fracture in a rock along which the two blocks have moved (been displaced) relative to each other**, parallel to the fracture plane |
| **Cause** | **tension or release of stress**: cooling contraction (columnar joints in basalt), unloading and uplift (sheet joints in granite), folding and regional stress | **shear or compressive stress** exceeding the strength of the rock (tension gives normal faults, compression gives reverse and thrust faults, shearing gives strike-slip faults) |
| **Evidence and size** | **no offset of beds**; occurs in **parallel sets** (systematic joints) and is of small to medium size | **offset of beds, veins or other features** (throw and heave), often with **fault rocks and slickensides**; can be many kilometres long and is the cause of **earthquakes** |

**(ii) Two features of fault zones.**

1. **Slickensides.** These are **smooth, polished, grooved (striated) surfaces on the fault plane**, formed by the **grinding of the two blocks against each other**. The **parallel scratches or ridges (slickenlines) show the direction of the last movement** along the fault, and a step on the surface (slickenfibres) shows the sense of movement. They are often coated with a thin film of quartz, calcite or chlorite.
2. **Fault breccia (and fault gouge).** This is the **zone of crushed rock along the fault plane**: **angular broken fragments of the wall rocks** held in a finer matrix and often **cemented by minerals deposited by circulating water** (quartz, calcite); where the grinding is finer the **crushed rock is a soft, clay-like powder called fault gouge**. The zone may be metres wide and is a path for ground water and ore-bearing fluids, with veins and mineralisation.

*(Other features: fault scarps, drag folds of the beds at the fault, mylonite, offset of rivers and ridges and linear valleys or springs along the fault line.)*

**(iii) Dating faults.**

- **Relative dating (by cross-cutting relations).** A fault is **younger than the youngest rock which it displaces** and **older than any rock or unconformity that cuts across it or covers it without being displaced**, e.g. an unfaulted later sedimentary bed or a later igneous dyke or intrusion which cuts the fault. The age of the fault is therefore **bracketed between these**.
- **Absolute (radiometric and other) dating.** Fault rocks and minerals which grew during movement (fine **micas and clays of the gouge, veins of calcite**, pseudotachylite) can be dated by **potassium-argon, argon-argon or uranium-lead methods** and by **fission-track dating** of minerals reset by the fault; **displaced young sediments, soils or organic remains** can be dated by **radiocarbon dating or luminescence**, and the age of a **fault scarp** by cosmogenic nuclides; **trenches across the fault** give the dates of recent earthquake offsets. **Historical and seismic records** give the dates of recent movements.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) List and locate TWO mineral deposits in Cameroon.

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two mineral deposits of Cameroon (each with its place):

1. **Bauxite (aluminium ore)**: the deposits of **Minim-Martap and Ngaoundal in the Adamawa Region** (central Cameroon), formed by **deep lateritic weathering** of aluminium-rich rocks in a warm, wet climate.
2. **Iron ore**: the deposit of **Mbalam in the East Region** (south-east Cameroon, near the border with the Republic of the Congo), in **Precambrian iron-rich rocks** of the Congo craton.

*(Other deposits that could be given: rutile at Akonolinga (Centre Region); cobalt-nickel-manganese at Lomié (East Region); gold in the Bétaré-Oya area (East Region); limestone at Figuil (North Region); and offshore oil and gas in the Rio del Rey basin.)*
